briefs.crm_archaeologist: A regional reference for Hohokam plainware, redware and Salado Polychrome in the central Phoenix Basin. Useful under deadline for the temper-based type definitions in Chapter 2, counts of wares by temporal component (Sacaton through Polvorón) in Table 2.1, and petrographic temper assignments for comparative collections in Chapter 3, which can support defensible attributions for sites in the same basin. The reference list is extensive and ready to cite. Treat sourcing results as interpretations tied to the sand composition zones this project defined.
briefs.graduate_student: The volume argues that space is the understudied dimension of Hohokam ceramic analysis and sets out to separate production areas using temper petrography, chemical analysis and a whole vessel study. Its synthesis builds a model of late Sedentary and Classic period production and exchange, claiming exchanges can be traced over distances as short as 5 km. Chapter 7 is a good place to examine interpretive disagreement: trade, migration, local production and competitive emulation have all been proposed to explain how Salado Polychrome spread. Worth testing how far the production-area model depends on the sand composition zones.
briefs.undergraduate_student: Archaeologists studied pottery from Pueblo Grande, a Hohokam village in what is now Phoenix, Arizona, to learn where pots were made and how they moved between communities. Much of the pottery looks similar, so they examined the tiny rock and sand grains mixed into the clay, called temper. Because different areas have different rocks, temper can hint at where a pot was made. The report compares pottery across several time periods and nearby sites, and discusses a well-known decorated style, Salado Polychrome, whose spread is still debated.
